Alaska, Maine and Georgia stay in the full forecast above and are tracked separately for evaluation.5.7 percentage pointsExpected average margin error across these 32 races, ignoring the direction of each miss.The middle 90% of simulated elections has an average error of 4.1 to 8.1 points.3.0 wrong top choices out of 32The middle 90% runs from 1 to 6 wrong choices in these same races.These are this model’s expectations, not observed errors or grades. The calculation preserves shared errors across races and uses this forecast’s own saved simulations. It does not combine simulations from different models.

All 35 predictions stay visible. The primary grade covers 32 candidate pairs.Alaska and Maine may require ranked-choice rounds; Georgia may require a runoff. They remain on the scoreboard with their own status. This grouping is chosen before election results arrive.The grade tests the margin and which of the two named candidates finishes ahead. It does not score the chance of every possible office winner.Why three races are tracked separatelyFor Alaska and Maine, the comparison requires an officially reported final round with exactly the two forecast candidates remaining. We will not invent transfers or substitute first-choice votes.For Georgia, the general-election count is used only if it decides the election without a runoff. Otherwise, the comparison waits for an actual runoff between the two forecast candidates.All comparisons concern the two named candidates’ votes. If another candidate wins the office, that is recorded separately; it does not erase known votes for the forecast pair. Certified tied pair counts can give a zero margin, but no winner-probability score.The primary grade needs eligible certified results for every one of its 32 races. A missing or disputed result stays pending; it is not dropped to produce a grade.
